Learning what we never observe

Maximum likelihood, expectation–maximization and hidden-variable models
Yuwen Huang
Advanced Machine Learning and Deep Learning · HKUST (Guangzhou)

→ next · ← back · F full screen · H keys
Why today

In real data, the key variable is often never written down

One method fits all four: expectation–maximization (EM). We learn it on two coins.

Warm-up · Retrieve before we build

Two questions from earlier lectures

A coin shows 7 heads in 10 flips. Our best guess of its heads chance?
Answer. 7/10: count, then divide. Today we prove that this is the maximum-likelihood answer.
Quadruple the Monte Carlo samples (Lecture 4): the error shrinks by a factor of…
Answer. 2: the error shrinks like 1/samples1/\sqrt{\text{samples}}1/samples​, and 4=2\sqrt4=24​=2.

Both answers return today: counting in EM's M-step, sampling in Monte Carlo EM.

The running example

The two-coin game: we see the flips, never the coin

We seethree records, HH, HT, TT (H = heads, T = tails).
Hiddenwhich coin made each record.
Goalthe heads chances θA\theta_AθA​ and θB\theta_BθB​ of the two coins.

Every idea today is first worked out on these three records, by hand.

The story

Eight questions; each answer raises the next

SectionQuestion on the coinsAnswer
1 CountingIf we are told each coin, what are θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​?count heads, divide
2 Hidden variablesNot told: how likely is a record, and which coin made it?a sum; Bayes' rule
3 EMCan we still count?yes, with soft labels
4 Why EM climbsDoes every round improve the fit?yes: a lower bound
5 MixturesWhat if coins become bell curves?the same EM clusters
6 Hidden chainsWhat if the coin switches between flips?forward–backward
7 Monte Carlo EMToo many hidden cases to add up?sample them
8 Trusting the fitIs the answer right, and the only one?restarts, counting test

Each section: idea → the coins, every step → theorem → where it is used today.

Learning objectives

By the end of today you can

1 · Countfit a model when nothing is hidden, and say why counting is the maximum-likelihood answer.
2 · Infercompute a record's probability with a hidden variable, and the posterior of that variable.
3 · Run EMby hand: the E-step (soft labels) and the M-step (count and divide).
4 · Provethat no EM round lowers the log-likelihood, with one inequality.
5 · RecogniseEM inside clustering, tokenizers, crowd labelling and reasoning models.
6 · Judgea fit: stuck starts, renamed labels, too many unknowns.

Six skills, one example: three records of two coin flips.

1 · Learning by counting · A · Idea

If the friend tells us the coin, we just count

Goal: learn θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​ from the flips. First the easy case: the coin of each record is told.

Coin A made HH and HT: 3 heads in 4 flips. Coin B made TT: 0 heads in 2 flips.

Guess: θA=34\theta_A=\tfrac34θA​=43​, θB=0\theta_B=0θB​=0. Why is counting the right answer?

1 · Learning by counting · B · On the coins

The likelihood of coin A's flips peaks at 3/4

Likelihood: the probability of what we saw, as a function of θA\theta_AθA​. A's flips H, H, H, T:

θA⋅θA⋅θA⋅(1−θA).\theta_A\cdot\theta_A\cdot\theta_A\cdot(1-\theta_A).θA​⋅θA​⋅θA​⋅(1−θA​).

Take logs (the peak stays put):

ℓ(θA)=3ln⁡θA+ln⁡(1−θA).\ell(\theta_A)=3\ln\theta_A+\ln(1-\theta_A).ℓ(θA​)=3lnθA​+ln(1−θA​).
Slope zero: 3θA−11−θA=0⇒3(1−θA)=θA⇒θA=34\dfrac{3}{\theta_A}-\dfrac{1}{1-\theta_A}=0\Rightarrow 3(1-\theta_A)=\theta_A\Rightarrow\cG{\theta_A=\tfrac34}θA​3​−1−θA​1​=0⇒3(1−θA​)=θA​⇒θA​=43​.

Maximum likelihood = the counted fraction, 3 of 4.

For any coin, the counted fraction maximizes the likelihood

the best heads chance is the fraction of heads seen.

Three coins, three peaks, each at its own counted fraction.

1 · Learning by counting · B · On the coins

Counting says coin B can never show heads

Coin B: 0 heads, 2 tails. Theorem 1: θB=02=0\theta_B=\tfrac{0}{2}=0θB​=20​=0.

Then a future record "B, then H" gets probability 0, and its log is −∞-\infty−∞. Two flips are too few to rule heads out.

Fix: pretend we also saw 1 head and 1 tail: θB=0+12+2=14\theta_B=\dfrac{0+1}{2+2}=\tfrac14θB​=2+20+1​=41​.

A zero count claims a certainty that two flips cannot support.

1 · Learning by counting · C · Theorem

Pseudo-counts are the average under a uniform prior

Why add exactly 1 and 1? Treat θ\thetaθ as random, every value in [0,1][0,1][0,1] equally likely before the flips.

Theorem 2 (Laplace's rule). Uniform prior, hhh heads, ttt tails:
E[θ∣flips]=h+1h+t+2.\mathbb E[\theta\mid\text{flips}]=\frac{h+1}{h+t+2}.E[θ∣flips]=h+t+2h+1​.
add one imagined head and one imagined tail, then count.
p(θ∣flips)∝θh(1−θ)tp(\theta\mid\text{flips})\propto\theta^h(1-\theta)^tp(θ∣flips)∝θh(1−θ)t
Bayes: prior 1 × likelihood.
E[θ]=∫01θh+1(1−θ)t∫01θh(1−θ)t=h+1h+t+2\mathbb E[\theta]=\dfrac{\int_0^1\theta^{h+1}(1-\theta)^t}{\int_0^1\theta^h(1-\theta)^t}=\dfrac{h+1}{h+t+2}E[θ]=∫01​θh(1−θ)t∫01​θh+1(1−θ)t​=h+t+2h+1​
∫01θa(1−θ)b=a! b!(a+b+1)!\int_0^1\theta^a(1-\theta)^b=\frac{a!\,b!}{(a+b+1)!}∫01​θa(1−θ)b=(a+b+1)!a!b!​; factorials cancel. ■\blacksquare■

Coin B: 0+12+2=14\tfrac{0+1}{2+2}=\tfrac142+20+1​=41​. Coin A: 3+14+2=23\tfrac{3+1}{4+2}=\tfrac234+23+1​=32​.

1 · Learning by counting · D · Today

Label smoothing is a pseudo-count for classifiers

An image classifier sees a cat photo. Training loss: −∑ktargetkln⁡predictionk-\sum_k\text{target}_k\ln\text{prediction}_k−∑k​targetk​lnpredictionk​.

Hard target (1,0,0)(1,0,0)(1,0,0): the loss −ln⁡p(cat)-\ln p(\text{cat})−lnp(cat) keeps falling as p(cat)→1p(\text{cat})\to1p(cat)→1: like θB=0\theta_B=0θB​=0, certainty is always rewarded.

Smoothed target (0.9,0.05,0.05)(0.9,0.05,0.05)(0.9,0.05,0.05) (Szegedy et al., 2016). Over-sure (0.98,0.01,0.01)(0.98,0.01,0.01)(0.98,0.01,0.01): loss 0.9⋅0.020+0.1⋅4.605=0.4790.9\cdot0.020+0.1\cdot4.605=0.4790.9⋅0.020+0.1⋅4.605=0.479. Prediction (0.9,0.05,0.05)(0.9,0.05,0.05)(0.9,0.05,0.05): 0.9⋅0.105+0.1⋅2.996=0.3940.9\cdot0.105+0.1\cdot2.996=0.3940.9⋅0.105+0.1⋅2.996=0.394, lower.

Like Laplace's imagined flips, the smoothed target stops the model from being too sure.

1 · Learning by counting · Connection

Next: the friend stops telling us the coin

Counting needs to know which coin made each flip. Now the label is hidden: "HH, by coin ?".

With θA=34\theta_A=\tfrac34θA​=43​, θB=14\theta_B=\tfrac14θB​=41​ and a fair pick, how likely is the record HH?
Answer. 5/16, between A's 9/16 and B's 1/16: we do not know which coin, so we average them.

A hidden coin turns one probability into a sum over the coins.

2 · Hidden variables · B · On the coins

Which coin made HH? Bayes' rule says A, with chance 9/10

Posterior: the chance of a coin after seeing the flips. Bayes' rule = a path's share of the total:

p(A∣HH)=932932+132=910.p(A\mid\text{HH})=\frac{\tfrac9{32}}{\tfrac9{32}+\tfrac1{32}}=\frac{9}{10}.p(A∣HH)=329​+321​329​​=109​.

HT: 33+3=12\tfrac{3}{3+3}=\tfrac123+33​=21​, a tie. TT: 11+9=110\tfrac{1}{1+9}=\tfrac1{10}1+91​=101​.

The posterior is a soft label: HH is 0.9 coin A and 0.1 coin B.

2 · Hidden variables · D · Today

A reasoning trace is a hidden coin

A language model is trained on question → answer pairs; the reasoning in between is never written down. Toy model: two possible reasonings.

coin gamereasoning model coin zzz↔reasoning zzz flips HH↔answer 14 p(A∣HH)=0.9p(A\mid\text{HH})=0.9p(A∣HH)=0.9↔p(z1∣14)=0.81p(z_1\mid 14)=0.81p(z1​∣14)=0.81

2 · Hidden variables · Connection

Next: count with soft labels

Section 1 counted with hard labels: HH is all A. Now we have soft labels: HH is 0.9 A.

How many heads should HH give to coin A?
Answer. 1.8: 0.9 of the record, and the record has 2 heads. This is EM's M-step.

Count fractions of records, then divide: expectation–maximization.

3 · Expectation–maximization · A · Idea

EM: guess the coins, soft-label the records, count, repeat

Goal: the θA,θB\theta_A,\theta_BθA​,θB​ that make HH, HT, TT most probable.

We need θ\thetaθ to label the records, and labels to count θ\thetaθ. Break the circle: start from a guess.

E-step (expectation): with the guess, the posterior soft-labels each record.

M-step (maximization): count as in Section 1, with fractions of records.

Each round uses only the flips and the last guess; no true coin is ever needed.

EM for any hidden-variable model

Definition (expectation–maximization; Dempster, Laird & Rubin, 1977). Start from θ0\theta_0θ0​. For t=0,1,2,…t=0,1,2,\dotst=0,1,2,…:
qt(n)(z)=pθt(z∣x(n))q_t^{(n)}(z)=p_{\theta_t}(z\mid x^{(n)})qt(n)​(z)=pθt​​(z∣x(n))
E-step: soft labels. Coins: 0.9, 0.5, 0.1.

M-step: fit as if each record were split by its soft labels. Coins: 2.3/3.

The M-step objective is a sum of logs of single paths: no log of a sum, so the arg max is easy (worked out below on the coins).

E: infer the hidden part. M: fit as if it were seen, with weights.

3 · Expectation–maximization · C · Theorem

On a tree model, the M-step is count-and-divide with fractions

Corollary (of Theorem 1). If pθ(x,z)p_\theta(x,z)pθ​(x,z) is a product of tables (a tree), the M-step sets each entry to
θentry=expected count of the caseexpected count of its condition.\theta_{\text{entry}}=\frac{\text{expected count of the case}}{\text{expected count of its condition}}.θentry​=expected count of its conditionexpected count of the case​.
each record adds its soft label to every case it may contain.

Why: ln⁡pθ(x,z)\ln p_\theta(x,z)lnpθ​(x,z) is a sum of log entries, so the objective separates entry by entry into Theorem 1's form: coin A's part was 2.3ln⁡θA+0.7ln⁡(1−θA)2.3\ln\theta_A+0.7\ln(1-\theta_A)2.3lnθA​+0.7ln(1−θA​).

Coin A: 2.3 expected heads of 3 expected flips. Coin B: 0.7 of 3.

3 · Expectation–maximization · D · Today

Crowd labelling: the true label is the hidden coin

Three people label one photo: cat, cat, dog. Nobody knows the truth. Each person is right with chance 0.8 (to be learned).

coin gamecrowd labelling coin↔true label two flips↔three people's labels heads chance θ\thetaθ↔each person's accuracy

M-step: person 3 said dog, so is right with chance 0.2 here; their accuracy = average over many photos (Dawid & Skene, 1979).

Used to clean noisy training labels: the two-coin game with people as coins.

3 · Expectation–maximization · Connection

Next: does every round improve the fit?

On the coins, ℓ\ellℓ rose every round: −4.000→−3.993→−3.990-4.000\to-3.993\to-3.990−4.000→−3.993→−3.990.

For any model and any start, can an EM round lower ℓ\ellℓ?
Answer. Never. The next section proves it with one picture and one inequality.

A guarantee, not luck: EM climbs.

4 · Why EM climbs · A · Idea

EM builds a curve under ℓ that touches it, then jumps to its top

Goal: show EM's ℓ\ellℓ never goes down.

Blue: ℓ\ellℓ along θB=1−θA\theta_B=1-\theta_AθB​=1−θA​. Dashed: the curve the E-step builds, always below ℓ\ellℓ, touching it at the current guess (red).

The M-step jumps to the dashed curve's top (circle). The blue curve there is at least as high: ℓ\ellℓ rose.

Below, touching, then the top: the three facts that make EM climb.

4 · Why EM climbs · D · Today

Variational autoencoders climb the same bound with a learned guess

For an image, the hidden zzz has hundreds of numbers: the posterior cannot be computed.

A variational autoencoder (Kingma & Welling, 2014) trains a network, the encoder, to output the guess q(z∣x)q(z\mid x)q(z∣x) in one pass.

Training raises Lemma 1's bound, here called the evidence lower bound (ELBO), in both the decoder (θ\thetaθ) and the encoder (qqq).

EM: the exact posterior as the guess. VAE: a learned guess that scales to images.

4 · Why EM climbs · Connection

Next: replace the coins by bell curves

Nothing in the proof used coins: only "observed xxx, hidden zzz, a model pθ(x,z)p_\theta(x,z)pθ​(x,z)".

Points on a line come from two groups, each a bell curve. In EM, what plays the coin?
Answer. The group: hidden, picked first, and the point is drawn from it. A Gaussian mixture.

Same E-step, same M-step: now it clusters.

5 · Mixture models · A · Idea

Same game, new records: numbers on a line instead of coin flips

Goal: find the groups in data with the same EM.

A friend picks group 1 or group 2 by a fair toss, then writes down a number near that group's centre. We see only the numbers: 0, 1, 4, 5.

Seethe four numbers
Hiddeneach number's group
Goalthe two centres

Coin ↔ group, flips ↔ a number. Every EM step will look exactly like the coins.

5 · Mixture models · A · Idea: k-means

k-means: give each point to its nearest centre, move each centre to its points' average

k-means (Lloyd, 1982), the most used clustering method, has two steps, repeated until nothing changes:

Assigneach point joins the nearest centre: a hard label, 1 or 0, never 0.989.
Moveeach centre goes to the plain average of the points that joined it.

Press One step: from the poor start (0, 1) it reaches centres 0.5 and 4.5 in two rounds.

5 · Mixture models · Appreciate

k-means or EM? Hard labels are fast; soft labels keep the doubt

k-meansFast and simple: one nearest-centre test per point. Assumes round groups of equal size. Point 2 is simply "group 1".
EM for a Gaussian mixtureKeeps the doubt: point 2 is "0.82 group 1". Also learns each group's width and weight, so groups may differ in size and shape.
Shared weaknessBoth only climb (Theorem 4; JJJ never rises), so a poor start can end at a poor answer. Fix: several starts, or spread-out starts (k-means++, Arthur & Vassilvitskii, 2007).
Common practiceRun k-means first for good centres, then EM to add widths, weights and soft labels.

One family: EM is k-means that admits uncertainty; k-means is EM that refuses it.

5 · Mixture models · D · Today

Vector search: k-means cells let a chatbot skip most of its documents

Task: each document is stored as a vector (a list of numbers; similar texts get nearby vectors). A question becomes a vector too; we need the stored vectors nearest to it (retrieval-augmented generation).

Slow way: compare the question with every stored vector. Picture: 240 comparisons.

k-means way (built once, in advance): cut the vectors into 4 cells. Then (1) compare with the 4 centres, (2) search only the nearest cell's 60 vectors: 64 comparisons, not 240.

At scale: 1,000,000 vectors, 1,000 cells of about 1,000: 1,000+1,000=2,0001{,}000+1{,}000=2{,}0001,000+1,000=2,000 comparisons, 500 times fewer (Jégou et al., 2011). Price: a neighbour just across a cell border can be missed.

k-means' "nearest centre" step, reused as an index: search a cell, not the library.

5 · Mixture models · D · Today

A mixture of experts: a router picks which networks handle each word

Setting: a language model reads text one token (a word or piece of a word) at a time. Instead of one huge network it has several smaller experts; running all of them for every token is expensive.

Router: a small network reads the token and gives each expert a weight, here (0.62,0.21,0.12,0.05)(0.62,0.21,0.12,0.05)(0.62,0.21,0.12,0.05), summing to 1: a mixture's group weights, but recomputed for every token, p(y∣x)=∑kπk(x) pk(y∣x)p(y\mid x)=\sum_k\pi_k(x)\,p_k(y\mid x)p(y∣x)=∑k​πk​(x)pk​(y∣x) (Jacobs et al., 1991).

Top-2: run only experts 1 and 2. Their weights sum to 0.62+0.21=0.830.62+0.21=0.830.62+0.21=0.83; rescale to sum to 1: 0.620.83=0.75\tfrac{0.62}{0.83}=0.750.830.62​=0.75, 0.210.83=0.25\tfrac{0.21}{0.83}=0.250.830.21​=0.25. Output =0.75⋅=0.75\cdot=0.75⋅expert 1 + 0.25⋅+\,0.25\cdot+0.25⋅expert 2. Experts 3 and 4 are never computed.

Scale: Mixtral has 8 experts and runs 2 per token, so each token uses about a quarter of the expert computation.

Expert ↔ group, router weight ↔ πk\pi_kπk​; keeping the top 2 is a nearly hard label, as in k-means.

5 · Mixture models · Connection

Next: the coin may switch between flips

So far one hidden group per record. Now the friend may switch coins between flips: one hidden coin per flip.

Three flips, each with its own hidden coin. How many coin sequences are there?
Answer. 8 =23=2^3=23. For 100 flips, 21002^{100}2100: too many to list.

Hidden chains: the sum over sequences, done step by step.

6 · Hidden chains · A · Idea

If the coin can switch between flips, the coins form a hidden chain

Goal: the posterior of each flip's coin, and p(flips)p(\text{flips})p(flips), without listing every sequence.

A hidden Markov model: each coin depends only on the coin before (Lecture 2's chain), each flip only on its own coin.

Flips H, H, T: which coin made flip 2?

To learn the switching game, run the same EM as for two coins

So far the rules were given (heads chances ¾, ¼; keep chance ¾). Now we only see flips and want to learn the rules. EM again: soft labels, then count and divide.

Why the extra label: "A at flip 1 with 0.8, A at flip 2 with 0.75" does not say whether the coin was kept; that needs the chance of the pair.

This EM for hidden chains is called Baum–Welch (Baum et al., 1970, before the name "EM" existed).

6 · Hidden chains · D · Today

Tokenizers learn where to cut words by EM over hidden cuts

A language model reads text in pieces (tokens). How "noon" should be cut is never written down; the tokenizer learns it (Kudo, 2018; SentencePiece).

coin chaintokenizer coin sequence↔a cut, e.g. no|on flips↔letters n, o, o, n heads chance↔piece probability

Allowed pieces: n, o, no, on, oo. A cut's chance = product of its pieces' probabilities. Below: one EM round by hand.

Speech recognition (CTC) does the same over hidden audio–letter alignments.

6 · Hidden chains · D · Today, what it means

Round 2: the cut no|on becomes almost certain

Same E-step with the new probabilities: a cut's chance = product of its pieces' probabilities.

cutchance with new probabilitiesposterior, round 1posterior, round 2
n|o|o|n0.222⋅0.121⋅0.121⋅0.222=0.00070.222\cdot0.121\cdot0.121\cdot0.222=0.00070.222⋅0.121⋅0.121⋅0.222=0.00070.0240.007
n|o|on0.222⋅0.121⋅0.303=0.0080.222\cdot0.121\cdot0.303=0.0080.222⋅0.121⋅0.303=0.0080.1220.073
n|oo|n0.222⋅0.051⋅0.222=0.00250.222\cdot0.051\cdot0.222=0.00250.222⋅0.051⋅0.222=0.00250.1220.022

Why no|on wins: each piece probability is below 1, so a cut with 2 pieces multiplies fewer small numbers than one with 4; then EM feeds back: likely cut → its pieces gain → the cut gets likelier.

What the tokenizer does with it: it cuts "noon" as no|on, 2 tokens instead of 4 letters, and pieces whose probability falls near 0 (like oo) are removed from the vocabulary.

On real text the same EM runs over millions of words, so a piece survives if it helps cut many words (Kudo, 2018).

6 · Hidden chains · Connection

Next: when even the shortcut is too big

Chains have forward–backward. A hidden reasoning text has astronomically many values and no chain shortcut.

How can we still get HH's soft label 0.9 without adding up the paths?
Answer. Replay and count: Monte Carlo, as in Lecture 4.

Replace the exact E-step by samples.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · A · Idea

Monte Carlo EM: keep the M-step, replace the exact E-step by random draws

Goal: run EM when the hidden variable has far too many values to add up.

exact EM (Section 3)Monte Carlo EM
E-step for HHshare of A =99+1=0.9=\tfrac{9}{9+1}=0.9=9+19​=0.9: needs the sum over all coinsdraw the coin 10 times from the posterior; A came up 9 times: share 910\tfrac9{10}109​

repeatwith the new guesswith the new guess: draw again

Why bother with coins? For a reasoning text zzz, the sum over all texts is impossible, but drawing one text is easy. Two questions follow: how to draw from the posterior, and how much noise the draws add.

Exact shares → fractions of draws. Everything else in EM stays.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · A · Idea

Replay the game and keep the runs that match the record

Goal: soft labels when the paths are too many to add up.

To label HH: replay the game with the current guess (toss for a coin, flip twice) and keep a run only if it shows HH.

No sum was computed: we only ran the model forward and compared. This is rejection sampling.

Kept runs are A in the ratio 9 : 1: exactly the posterior 0.9.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · B · On the coins

A few draws give noisy counts; many draws approach the exact split

Each dot: one draw of the coin from the posterior (for HH: A with chance 0.9). The fraction of A's replaces the exact share in the M-step. Press 1, 10, 100, 1000 draws per record.

More draws ⇒ the new θA\theta_AθA​ wobbles less around the exact 0.767.

7 · Monte Carlo EM · D · Today

Learning to reason from answers is the replay-and-keep game

coin gamereasoning model toss for a coin↔write a reasoning flips show HH?↔answer correct? keep the run↔keep the reasoning

Example: the model writes 4 reasonings for "2 + 3 × 4"; one ends in 14 (correct). Keep that one: a posterior draw, as with HH.

M-step: fine-tune on the kept reasonings, then repeat. Self-Taught Reasoner, STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022); Reinforced Self-Training with EM, ReST-EM (Singh et al., 2023).

Replay, keep matches, train: Monte Carlo EM with a reasoning as the coin.

8 · Trusting the fit · C · Theorem

The counting test: unknowns must not exceed what the data can tell

Theorem 8 (counting test). If the model has more unknowns than the data distribution has free numbers, the parameters are not identifiable: a curve or surface of settings gives the same data distribution.
3 unknowns cannot be read off 2 numbers.

Why: a smooth map from 3 numbers to 2 must send whole curves to single points (rank theorem). Three flips give 3 free numbers = 3 unknowns, and the coins become identifiable up to swapping names (Allman, Matias & Rhodes, 2009).

Fix a ridge by observing more per record, not by running EM longer.

8 · Trusting the fit · D · Today

Do learned hidden codes mean anything?

A variational autoencoder's code zzz is a hidden coin with many numbers, and we hope each axis means one thing (pose, colour).

Tiny example: rotate every code by 90°, (z1,z2)→(−z2,z1)(z_1,z_2)\to(-z_2,z_1)(z1​,z2​)→(−z2​,z1​), and let the decoder undo the rotation first. Same images, same ℓ\ellℓ, since the code prior (round) does not change. Like renaming A and B.

So axes cannot be learned from images alone (Locatello et al., 2019). But an extra observed variable, such as time, can pin them (Hyvärinen & Morioka, 2016): the third flip again.

More observations, not more training, make hidden codes identifiable.

Research questions

Open questions at the frontier

Reasoning as a hidden coinOn the coins, 10 of 32 replays were kept. On a hard question maybe 1 in 1,000 reasonings is correct: most draws are wasted. How can we draw good reasonings directly (Phan et al., 2023)?
The highest peakFrom (12,12)(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)(21​,21​) EM is stuck; from elsewhere it finds a peak, not always the highest. When does a cheap first estimate (spectral methods) start EM close enough (Zhang et al., 2016)?
Meaningful codesTwo flips could not pin down three unknowns; a third flip could. Which extra observations make a deep network's hidden code identifiable (Hyvärinen & Morioka, 2016)?

Each is today's coin game with a much larger hidden coin.
